title: How do energy companies and utilities make money, and what matters in their cases?
description: Energy and utilities economics for case interviews: regulated returns, generation costs, capacity, the energy transition and rooftop solar, with a worked…
hook: Energy cases are increasingly common because the energy transition is reshaping the industry. Utilities are often regulated, investments are huge and long-lived, and new technologies like solar and batteries are changing who makes money.
body:
The main businesses

  • Generation: making electricity from gas, wind, solar, nuclear and more.
  • Networks: the grid that moves power, often regulated monopolies earning an allowed return.
  • Retail: selling energy to homes and businesses, a competitive, thin-margin business.

Long-lived investments

Power plants and grids last decades, so payback and NPV matter a lot in these cases.

A worked example: rooftop solar's effect on a utility

A utility sells 10,000 GWh a year to homes. If 10% of homes install solar and cut their grid use by 40%, sales fall by 10% × 40% = 4%, or 400 GWh. But the grid's costs are mostly fixed, so the same costs are spread over fewer units, pushing prices up for everyone else and encouraging even more solar.

Typical energy case questions

  • How should a utility respond to rooftop solar?
  • Should we invest in a wind farm or battery storage?
  • Should a city or government back a new nuclear plant?
  • How should an oil company plan for falling demand?
